message: What VA benefits am I eligible for?
answer:
I can't determine which benefits you're eligible for; VA decides that based on your service and records. Here are the main areas to look at:

- **Education:** The Post-9/11 GI Bill provides up to 36 months of education benefits. [D01]

- **Disability compensation:** VA disability compensation is a monthly, tax-free payment for veterans with conditions connected to their military service. [D05]

- **Health care:** Most veterans who served in the active military and were discharged under conditions other than dishonorable can apply for VA health care. [D08]

- **Home loans:** The VA home loan guaranty helps eligible veterans, service members and some surviving spouses buy, build or refinance a home. [D10]

- **Free help:** Veterans Service Organizations (VSOs), state and county veteran service officers, and other VA-accredited representatives can help you file and manage claims at no cost. [D19]

<source id="D01" type="official" last_reviewed="2025-03-01">
The Post-9/11 GI Bill provides up to 36 months of education benefits. You generally qualify with at least 90 days of aggregate active-duty service after September 10, 2001, or if you were discharged with a service-connected disability after 30 days. Your benefit level is 40% to 100% depending on how long you served.

When you use it at an approved school, the benefit can pay tuition and fees directly to the school, a monthly housing allowance based on the school's ZIP code, and a yearly books and supplies stipend. Benefit levels and rates are set by VA; confirm your own percentage by applying for a Certificate of Eligibility.
</source>
<source id="D05" type="official" last_reviewed="2025-02-20">
VA disability compensation is a monthly, tax-free payment for veterans with conditions connected to their military service. VA assigns a disability rating from 0% to 100% in 10% steps; the rating is based on the evidence in your claim.

Payment rates change every year on December 1 with the cost-of-living adjustment. Always check the current-year rate table on VA.gov for the amount that matches your rating and dependents. The effective date of your benefit is usually the date VA receives your claim. Filing an Intent to File (VA Form 21-0966) can protect that date for up to one year while you gather evidence.
</source>
<source id="D08" type="official" last_reviewed="2025-01-30">
Most veterans who served in the active military and were discharged under conditions other than dishonorable can apply for VA health care. VA places enrolled veterans into priority groups 1 through 8, which affect copays and wait for some services.

You can apply online at VA.gov, by phone, by mail, or in person at a VA medical center. Veterans who served in locations with certain toxic exposures may qualify for enrollment under expanded eligibility rules (see the PACT Act overview). Having a VA disability rating can place you in a higher priority group.
</source>
<source id="D10" type="official" last_reviewed="2025-04-02">
The VA home loan guaranty helps eligible veterans, service members and some surviving spouses buy, build or refinance a home. Most VA-backed loans do not require a down payment and do not require private mortgage insurance.

You start by requesting a Certificate of Eligibility (COE). Most borrowers pay a one-time VA funding fee, but veterans who receive VA disability compensation are exempt from the funding fee. VA does not make the loan itself: private lenders set interest rates and credit requirements, so compare offers from more than one lender.
</source>
<source id="D19" type="official" last_reviewed="2025-02-12">
Veterans Service Organizations (VSOs), state and county veteran service officers, and other VA-accredited representatives can help you file and manage claims at no cost. You can search for an accredited representative on VA.gov.

It is against the law for anyone to charge you a fee for help preparing or filing an initial claim. Be careful of companies that promise higher ratings in exchange for money.
</source>
<question>What VA benefits am I eligible for?</question>

message: Can I transfer my GI Bill to my daughter? I separated in 2024.
answer: Unfortunately, no. A transfer has to be requested while you are still serving, through DoD's milConnect, and it cannot be requested after you have separated or retired [D04]. Since you separated in 2024, a transfer to a family member is no longer possible under these rules. A separate program, Dependents' Educational Assistance (DEA), covers children and spouses of veterans who died or are permanently and totally disabled because of a service-connected condition; VA decides who qualifies [D24].

VA disability compensation is a monthly, tax-free payment for veterans with conditions connected to their military service. VA assigns a disability rating from 0% to 100% in 10% steps; the rating is based on the evidence in your claim.

Payment rates change every year on December 1 with the cost-of-living adjustment. Always check the current-year rate table on VA.gov for the amount that matches your rating and dependents. The effective date of your benefit is usually the date VA receives your claim. Filing an Intent to File (VA Form 21-0966) can protect that date for up to one year while you gather evidence.
</source>
